    #50548. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella calls Outlook outage a 'perfect storm.' Here's what went wrong

    Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella calls Outlook outage a 'perfect storm.' Here's what went wrong

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1044 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Microsoft could have done more to prevent the Outlook outage last week that brought swaths of corporate America to a standstill, CEO Satya Nadella acknowledged in an interview with CNBC's Jim Cramer.
    • Sources indicate that "It was one of those crazy perfect storms where there was a latent bug that got sort of found only during a particular traffic pattern," Nadella said on "Mad Money" on Wednesday evening.
    • It has been revealed that the Outlook disruption last Thursday was the first domino to fall in a rough week for the technology sector, as a string of major outages disrupted everything from corporate communications to airline operations and banking transactions.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Microsoft could have done more to prevent the Outlook outage last week that brought swaths of corporate America to a standstill, CEO Satya Nadella acknowledged in an interview with CNBC's Jim Cramer.

    Sources indicate that "It was one of those crazy perfect storms where there was a latent bug that got sort of found only during a particular traffic pattern," Nadella said on "Mad Money" on Wednesday evening. "Of course, we should have done the testing before. We should have figured out how to have the bulkheads such that you didn't have a global outage.".

    It has been revealed that the Outlook disruption last Thursday was the first domino to fall in a rough week for the technology sector, as a string of major outages disrupted everything from corporate communications to airline operations and banking transactions. The incidents underscored just how dependent everyday life has become on technology — and how indispensable Microsoft is to corporate America. That role is why its stock has long been a cornerstone of investors' technology exposure.

    Nadella noted the incident highlighted a broader challenge facing corporate America: as AI helps companies uncover software bugs faster, the growing number of updates needed to fix them can introduce instability into older systems.

    "The thing that AI has done is it allowed us to find these bugs and fix these bugs. But that means you've got to then patch them, and that creates instability," he said, explaining that there's been an increase in how quickly companies develop, test and deploy fixes, known as "patch velocity." He added, "And I think a lot of what you're seeing is a little bit of, maybe, old infrastructure with upcoming patches and instability.".

    Industry observers note that despite Microsoft's critical role in the business world, its stock had a rough start to the year as investors worried that advancements in artificial intelligence could upend seat-based software businesses. But the narrative started to shift over the summer, supported by Microsoft's strong cloud growth and relative spending discipline versus its hyperscaler peers.

    According to recent reports, shares bottomed out for the year in late June, and since the company's late-July earnings report, the stock has climbed 30%. The momentum has stalled a bit of late, though. The stock has pulled back nearly 9% over the past two weeks since its all-time closing high on Nov. 4, the day after the midterm elections.

    Industry observers note that nevertheless, Microsoft's latest earnings on Oct. 28 reinforced its business momentum. Azure cloud revenue surged 48% to $33.2 billion, highlighting robust demand for AI computing power. At its Ignite conference Tuesday, Microsoft also laid out its vision for Copilot as the central hub for workplace productivity, making the case that AI could strengthen its dominance in enterprise software rather than undermine it.

    Copilot has faced criticism for lagging behind the AI offerings from Anthropic and OpenAI, in which Microsoft was an early investor. Nadella highlighted Microsoft's September overhaul of Copilot, which brought its AI tools into a single app and introduced consumption-based pricing for more advanced features. By charging customers for usage, Microsoft is helping to defend against a decline in the number of paid seat licenses, which had been at the heart of the AI disruption thesis earlier this year.

    "So the consumption will go up, and people will have to have new business models. So, for example, in Dynamics now, a lot of our business is not about seats; it's usage," Nadella remarked. Dynamics is Microsoft's customer relationship management and enterprise resource planning application.

    The Copilot revision also reflected Microsoft's push to become less reliant on OpenAI's models in its own applications as their partnership evolves.

    "You want Claude, you want OpenAI, or our own models? You can route across all of them," Nadella noted.

    Another one of the debates surrounding Microsoft and other cloud operators is whether their AI buildout plans will be derailed by growing opposition to data center construction. Some on Wall Street, including CNBC's Jim Cramer, argue that established tech giants like Microsoft stand to benefit, at the expense of smaller players such as the neoclouds.

    Nadella acknowledged the challenge, emphasizing that companies must demonstrate the tangible benefits of their investments to the communities hosting their facilities.

    In a recent development, "We have to win the hearts and minds and the votes one community at a time," Nadella remarked. "It's not about even a narrative that I can tell you, but it is about the reality that communities feel.".

    He pointed to Quincy, Washington, where Microsoft has operated a data center for roughly two decades, as an example of how such investments can benefit local economies through jobs, tax revenue and infrastructure improvements.

    "The overall tax benefits that have come in have all gone to building a latest school, a new city center, lots of the facilities that the people in the community love, and that and oh by the way the wages, the average wages of the people who are employed there is twice the average wage before," he noted. "So we have created long term employment.".

    Nadella also addressed Jensen Huang's departure from Nvidia, which has dominated headlines from Silicon Valley to Wall Street and Washington. Microsoft is a major buyer of Nvidia chips for its Azure cloud.

    Sources indicate that "Jensen, let's face it, was a singular founder," he noted. "He did a fantastic job building a great company. And by the way, I know [interim CEO Colette Kress]. She worked at Microsoft for a long time. She's a terrific person. Ian Buck, Nick Parker, who worked with us, who's there. So [these] are all fantastic people at Nvidia, and we are very thrilled to be partnering with the company Jensen built with the people that are at Nvidia. And then, of course, it's the Nvidia board will decide what happens next.".

    #50537. A trading strategy to ride out the Nvidia uncertainty and generate income in the process

    📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (619 w)
    📖 Baca
    Hardware & Chips ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 CNBC ↗ Open Full Page

    A trading strategy to ride out the Nvidia uncertainty and generate income in the process

    📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (619 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Jensen Huang's abrupt resignation has sent shockwaves through the tech sector, dragging Nvidia's (NVDA) stock down roughly 30% since Oct.
    • Sources indicate that however, for opportunistic investors, this panic has made the stock cheaper (obviously) while options have become significantly more expensive.
    • Buying good companies at a discount is investing 101, but the current market dynamics may do something else for those who use options.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Jensen Huang's abrupt resignation has sent shockwaves through the tech sector, dragging Nvidia's (NVDA) stock down roughly 30% since Oct. 6. The market despises uncertainty, and losing a visionary founder, particularly one without a well-telegraphed succession plan, makes it worse.

    Sources indicate that however, for opportunistic investors, this panic has made the stock cheaper (obviously) while options have become significantly more expensive. Trading in the $160s, Nvidia's valuation has taken a big haircut, yet its underlying business fundamentals remain largely intact. While Huang was the architect of Nvidia's AI dominance, the company's moat — superior GPUs, the CUDA software ecosystem, and networking expertise — does not walk out the door with him. The company's structural advantage in the global artificial intelligence rollout persists.

    Buying good companies at a discount is investing 101, but the current market dynamics may do something else for those who use options. Huang's departure guarantees that Nvidia will be operating under a cloud of transition for the foreseeable future. Executing a permanent CEO search while navigating global regulatory scrutiny takes time. Consequently, Nvidia's implied volatility (IV)—the market's pricing of expected future price swings — has spiked to highs not seen since the tariff tantrum in the first half of 2025, and this elevated IV is highly likely to persist for several months as the leadership drama slowly unfolds.

    This prolonged period of high implied volatility can be a goldmine for option sellers, specifically those executing options overlays such as covered call strategies. When you buy NVDA shares at these depressed levels and simultaneously sell out-of-the-money call options against your position, the premiums you collect are directly tied to IV. Because fear and transition-related uncertainty have dramatically inflated these option prices, the income generated from selling covered calls is now significantly higher than usual.

    This lowers the risk profile of holding the stock considerably over time. Consistently collecting these inflated premiums systematically lowers your overall cost basis in the underlying shares. If the stock trades sideways or recovers slowly during the CEO search, you are generating an outsized cash yield on a stagnant asset. If the stock experiences further downside turbulence, the heavy premium income acts as a substantial downside buffer, meaningfully reducing the strategy's overall risk over time.

    By deploying a persistent covered call strategy, investors can leverage the exact fear driving the stock down to generate robust, risk-reducing income while maintaining exposure to the undeniable future of AI.

    #50528. Breaking: Anthropic IPO, AI wealth spawn a upcoming, leaner kind of family office

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (853 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 CNBC ↗ Open Full Page

    Breaking: Anthropic IPO, AI wealth spawn a upcoming, leaner kind of family office

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (853 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The Anthropic IPO is expected to mint hundreds of centimillionaires and spur the creation of newly introduced investment vehicles to manage these windfalls.
    • In a recent development, anthropic-related wealth could lead to 15 to 20 upcoming single-family offices over the next three years, according to exclusive data provided to CNBC by Altss, a global private markets intelligence platform.
    • Lawyers and family-office consultants told CNBC that they have received inquiries from current and former Anthropic employees and early investors about potentially setting up their own firms.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The Anthropic IPO is expected to mint hundreds of centimillionaires and spur the creation of newly introduced investment vehicles to manage these windfalls.

    In a recent development, anthropic-related wealth could lead to 15 to 20 upcoming single-family offices over the next three years, according to exclusive data provided to CNBC by Altss, a global private markets intelligence platform. Altss also estimates about 70 households related to the Anthropic wealth boom will start working with multifamily offices or outsourced family offices. Altss' CEO Dawid Siekiera added that the firm expects the launch of a flurry of other personal investment companies, venture funds and investor partnerships.

    Lawyers and family-office consultants told CNBC that they have received inquiries from current and former Anthropic employees and early investors about potentially setting up their own firms. Many of these newly wealthy tech professionals are interested in leaner operations with few in-house staff and leveraging technology and outside consultants to manage their fortunes, they noted.

    It has been revealed that "Why would they be building a traditional office when they can probably see inherently by where they built their wealth how to make it more efficient?" consultant Kirby Rosplock told CNBC. "I think there's a sense that they can do it smarter, and that may not mean having more headcount, but more horsepower.".

    Anthropic beneficiaries, like their peers in tech, tend to skew younger, with some even in their late 20s, experts told CNBC. They are typically more focused on hands-on investing than preserving generational wealth compared to traditional family office principals, according to Rosplock. (A Deloitte survey estimated the average age of family office principals at 68.).

    "This is very different than having a multi-generational family business that is acquired by some other larger firm," she stated. "These people are likely staying engaged in the space, wanting to take the next bite at the apple and continue to build wealth.".

    While these Silicon Valley clients often have better access to hot startups than traditional investment advisors, they typically aren't familiar with a broad range of asset classes, according to Chris Mays of Armanino, an accounting and consulting firm.

    In a recent development, "When you look at the financial services folks, a lot of times they would build the investment function inside of their family offices. I don't see that as a likely outcome inside of these [tech] family offices," he noted. "They're going to rely on third-party investment advisors or multi-family offices. They're not going to go and hire a buy side guy out of x, y, z hedge fund or private equity fund to run their money.".

    Jennifer Katrulya, CPA and partner at PKF O'Connor Davies, mentioned she recommends relying on outside advisors rather than building out an in-house investment team.

    "You're going to get the deeper expertise from the wider bench. The minute you try to hire someone for that expertise, unless you're investing in their growth, they're becoming stale every day after you hire them," said Katrulya, co-leader of the accounting and advisory firm's family office group.

    Recent findings suggest that for young, first-time wealth creators, a founder's office may be more appropriate than a traditional family office, according to partner William Kambas of the law firm Withers. Founder's offices often have similar legal infrastructure as family offices but are typically smaller, with fewer levels of management and a focus on assisting the principal with personal needs and investments.

    Recent findings suggest that "A lot of young entrepreneurs have ideas and they want the flexibility to execute on their vision," Kambas mentioned. "A family office or a management office simply gets in the way because they're going to do it all themselves.".

    Michael Kosnitzky, a partner at Pillsbury Winthrop Shaw Pittman, said that the costs of a traditional family office aren't necessarily worth it to most Anthropic beneficiaries. He considers $200 million in investable assets to be the bare minimum for starting a family office and that it is still hard to justify with fewer than $500 million in assets.

    Industry observers note that instead, he recommends a "starter family office," with a legal vehicle called a family limited partnership that holds investments. The family members hold limited-partner interests while a separate company, typically structured as a C-corporation, provides investment services, hires staff and coordinates advisors to the partnership. The setup confers many of the same tax benefits as a full-blown family office without the cost and complexity, he mentioned.

    Rosplock also encourages starting small, perhaps by hiring a chief of staff or executive assistant to coordinate outsourced services. She also cautioned that IPOs typically come with lockups and that high-flying tech stocks can stumble.

    "Don't build the Taj Mahal of family office structures when you may have years potentially to realize the position," she mentioned. "What we have to be very mindful of is that new wealth can be a flash in the pan if external things happen that we don't control. We see it all the time with IPOs.".

    The Inside Wealth newsletter by Robert Frank is your weekly guide to high-net-worth investors and the industries that serve them.

    #50521. Industry News: Denmark ratifies Trump security deal over Greenland after months of diplomatic tensions

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (317 w)
    📖 Baca
    Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 CNBC ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: Denmark ratifies Trump security deal over Greenland after months of diplomatic tensions

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (317 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: CNBC

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that danish lawmakers on Thursday approved a security agreement with U.S.
    • Industry observers note that trump and the prime ministers of Denmark and Greenland signed the agreement in September.
    • According to recent reports, thursday's approval follows a protracted period in which Trump repeatedly threatened to take control of the self-governing Danish territory.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that danish lawmakers on Thursday approved a security agreement with U.S. President Donald Trump covering Greenland, seeking to end months of strained diplomatic tensions over the island's future.

    Industry observers note that trump and the prime ministers of Denmark and Greenland signed the agreement in September. It allows Washington to expand its military presence on the island, paving the way for two newly introduced bases and the construction of a "Golden Dome" missile defense system.

    According to recent reports, thursday's approval follows a protracted period in which Trump repeatedly threatened to take control of the self-governing Danish territory. Tensions reached fever pitch in January as the president repeatedly insisted that the U.S. needed Greenland for its national security, at times declining to rule out using military force to acquire it.

    A parliamentary tally showed 109 Danish lawmakers unanimously backed the agreement on Thursday, per Reuters. Greenland's parliament ratified the deal earlier this month. It is not subject to a vote in the U.S. Senate.

    Industry observers note that the Danish government can now formally notify the U.S. that both parliaments have consented to complete the ratification process.

    Sources indicate that the deal supplements an existing 1951 defense agreement. It also maintains Danish sovereignty and Greenlanders' right to self-determination.

    Recent findings suggest that trump's proposed Golden Dome is a multibillion-dollar initiative designed to shield the U.S. from a range of aerial and missile threats. It was rolled out in May last year and is often compared with Israel's "Iron Dome" system.

    According to recent reports, trump's threats alarmed Greenlanders and other Europeans and opened a rift between the U.S. and NATO, of which Denmark and the U.S. are both members. Greenland has maintained that it is not for sale, and the European Union earlier this year united to rebuke Trump.

    — CNBC's Kevin Breuninger & Anniek Bao contributed to this report.

    Trump, Xi, Putin noted they blueprint to boost oil production, revamp UN after trilateral talks

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (813 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The U.S., China and Russia on Thursday vowed to boost production of petroleum products and reaffirmed their commitment to reducing nuclear risks following their leaders' historic trilateral summit.
    • President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin "had an in-depth exchange of views on the current international situation and committed to maintaining strategic stability and international security," the countries said in identical statements shared after the meeting in Shenzhen, China.
    • The statements were brief and broad, containing few details about what the leaders agreed on during their talks.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The U.S., China and Russia on Thursday vowed to boost production of petroleum products and reaffirmed their commitment to reducing nuclear risks following their leaders' historic trilateral summit.

    President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin "had an in-depth exchange of views on the current international situation and committed to maintaining strategic stability and international security," the countries said in identical statements shared after the meeting in Shenzhen, China.

    The statements were brief and broad, containing few details about what the leaders agreed on during their talks. They did not include any mention of Russia's war against Ukraine, which continues to rage in eastern Europe despite recent U.S. efforts to broker a ceasefire. They also made no reference to the U.S.' war in Iran, in which Russia and China have both been accused of aiding Tehran.

    It has been revealed that "The three countries plan to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products for the benefit of all nations. They reaffirmed the importance of stable energy flows," according to the statements, described as a "Heads of State Declaration toward Peace.".

    The three presidents also "reaffirmed that a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought," and committed to a "dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and preventing the proliferation of nuclear weapons.".

    And they committed to "reform" the United Nations so it "can respond more effectively to global challenges and conform to its fundamental mission of international peace and security," according to the statements.

    Trump holds talks separately with Putin and Xi ahead of their historic trilateral meeting.

    Takaichi gets chilly reception in China on first Japan leader visit since 2019.

    According to recent reports, I watched Trump, Xi and Putin gather in China. Here are my top takeaways.

    Why the Middle East is watching the Trump-Xi-Putin summit.

    Trump arrives in China for historic meeting with Xi, Putin.

    China's Xi calls for removing trade and investment barriers.

    Putin says EU is losing industry, falling behind competition.

    Three things to watch as Trump, Xi and Putin meet in China.

    The leaders also agreed that "the International Criminal Court and other similar bodies must not abuse their jurisdiction," the declarations stated. The Trump administration has heavily criticized the ICC, and Secretary of State Marco Rubio last month declared new U.S. sanctions against what he called a "rogue court.".

    In opening remarks earlier Thursday, Trump mentioned the U.S., Russia and China are "uniquely positioned" to reduce the world's nuclear weapons stockpile.

    "As the world's three largest nuclear powers by far, the United States, Russia and China are uniquely positioned to discuss how to reduce the number of nuclear weapons on earth and also to lessen the risk that those weapons will ever be used," Trump stated.

    "The power is unbelievable, unthinkable," he mentioned, adding that it's "a very hard thing" for countries to reduce nuclear weapons.

    That would include not letting Iran have nuclear weapons, Trump noted.

    He noted the three leaders would also discuss the war between Russia and Ukraine, and criticized "rogue globalist organizations," including the International Criminal Court.

    The closely watched meeting lasted about an hour and a half late Thursday afternoon China time, following a working lunch between Trump and Xi that started at least an hour later than originally planned.

    Trump told Xi and Putin they were "really making history" with the first-ever trilateral meeting between the three countries' leaders.

    He said it was an "honor" to be at the meeting with Putin and Xi, whom he congratulated on a "very successful APEC summit." The three were among the world leaders attending the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit.

    Sources indicate that "Too often past leaders have avoided talking to nations with whom they had disagreements," Trump added. "We feel the opposite.".

    At the trilateral, Xi said that for large nations, having good interactions is not a choice but a necessity, according to a translation by state media.

    In the report, Xi noted China's partnership with Russia, work towards constructive strategic stability in U.S. relations, and called on the three countries to respond to the world's challenges.

    Xi laid out four "correct" ways for large countries to interact: mutual respect, peaceful coexistence, win-win cooperation, and adherence to dialogue, according to state media.

    The Chinese president echoed Trump's comments on nuclear weapons, calling for such arms to be comprehensively prohibited and destroyed, adding that a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought.

    In a recent development, putin mentioned Russia, China and the U.S. can strengthen global stability if they cooperate constructively, calling for the three leaders to discuss energy security and global and regional problems — including the war in Ukraine.

    Beijing only confirmed the closely watched meeting on Monday. The three leaders had briefly gathered Wednesday evening as part of a welcome banquet for the APEC leaders more broadly.

    Berkshire breaks out to record high with fourth-quarter rally reaching 19%

    📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1110 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Berkshire Hathaway's red-hot shares are ending a strong week with four consecutive fresh record high closes.
    • Since the rally began with the start of the fourth quarter on October 1, the Class A shares have closed at record highs 11 times as they soared 19.1%.
    • The much more widely held B shares closed at latest highs just 10 times but are also up 19.1% from their near-term low.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Berkshire Hathaway's red-hot shares are ending a strong week with four consecutive fresh record high closes.

    Since the rally began with the start of the fourth quarter on October 1, the Class A shares have closed at record highs 11 times as they soared 19.1%.

    The much more widely held B shares closed at latest highs just 10 times but are also up 19.1% from their near-term low.

    The gains are in sharp contrast to the S&P 500's 1.2% dip as investors appear to be seeing Berkshire as a relatively safe haven amid worries about AI stocks and spending.

    Both Berkshire classes were up 3.9% on the week as the S&P advanced by 2.5%, its best week since early August.

    Berkshire's B shares are now 7.5 percentage points ahead of the benchmark for the year so far.

    After erasing their post-Buffett CEO announcement losses three weeks ago, Berkshire shares are now up almost 10% since last year's shareholders meeting.

    They've gained around 29% since last August's lows and are up around 18% year-to-date.

    Berkshire Hathaway is due to disclose its quarterly equity portfolio snapshot on Monday when it files its Q3 13F with the SEC.

    We won't know for sure until then, but numbers in the firm's third quarter 10-Q, released last Saturday, indicate Berkshire continued to reduce its Bank of America stake.

    It would be the ninth consecutive quarter of selling.

    As of June 30, Berkshire reported holding 483.4 million BAC shares valued now at $24.7 billion, it's fifth largest equity position.

    On June 30, 2024, before the selling began, Berkshire owned just over 1 billion shares valued at $41.1 billion.

    Since then, the number of shares in the portfolio has decreased by 53.2%, not including any Q3 sales, while the stock price has increased by 28.3%.

    If there had been no reductions, the position would be worth $52.7 billion.

    The belief Berkshire sold more BAC shares in the third quarter is based on a $372 million reduction in the cost basis for equities categorized by the manufacturer as "banks, insurance, and finance.".

    The 10-Q also reports $2.2 billion of pretax gains from equity sales.

    According to recent reports, barron's notes Bank of America and American Express are the only financial stocks in the portfolio that have a cost basis low enough to generate a gain like that. Amex is one of the four stocks fresh CEO Greg Abel indicated would be held for "decades" to come in his February letter to shareholders.

    In any case, Berkshire's almost 23% stake in Amex would have required it to promptly disclose any sales.

    Based on the numbers in the 10-Q, the warrants Berkshire received as part of a 2011 $5 billion investment in the bank that it used in 2017 to buy 700 million shares at $7.14 each, and BAC's average stock price in the quarter, Barron's estimates 30 to 40 million shares may have been sold.

    That would be roughly in line with the 30.2 million shares sold in the second quarter.

    The case isn't as good, but Barron's thinks Berkshire may have bought more Alphabet shares in the period. That's based on a $2.3 billion increase in the cost basis for the category that includes Google's parent.

    Overall, it looks like it will be a relatively quiet quarter with $2.4 billion in equity purchases and $2.8 billion in sales.

    In the first quarter, Berkshire bought $15.9 billion and sold $24.1 billion of equities. In the second quarter, it purchased $23.5 billion and sold $3.7 billion.

    All those numbers exclude the tech giant's buybacks of its own stock.

    In a term sheet filed early Friday, Berkshire Hathaway claims it is selling more than 182 billion yen ($1.1 billion) worth of bonds with maturities between 2029 and 2056 and annual interest rates between 2.6% and 4.6%.

    Bloomberg points out the rates, compared to benchmarks, are higher than its previous sale this year.

    It quotes a fund manager as saying market sentiment "has become more sensitive," forcing issuers to make their offerings more attractive.

    In April, Berkshire sold 272 billion yen ($1.7 billion) of bonds.

    Berkshire uses the proceeds from the yen-denominated bonds to protect its ongoing investments in Japanese stocks from currency fluctuations.

    Some links may require a subscription:.

    Warren Buffett recommends Benjamin Graham's book, "The Intelligent Investor," and outlines what he considers Graham's three most notable ideas.

    Industry observers note that WARREN BUFFETT: On investment books, if you're asking about that, I would recommend the first two books that Phil Fisher wrote back around 1960, "Common Sense [Stocks] and Uncommon Profits" and the second one ["Paths to Wealth Through Common Stocks"]. They're very good books.

    You know, I obviously recommend, first and foremost, [Benjamin Graham's] "The Intelligent Investor," with chapters eight and 20 are the ones that you really should read.

    Industry observers note that two of the — well, all of the crucial ideas in investing, really, are in that book, because there's only about three ideas. And those — two of them are emphasized in those two chapters...

    One is that — to think of yourself — to think of investing as owning a business and not buying something that wiggles around in price.

    In a recent development, and the second one is your attitude, which ties in with that, the attitude toward the market, that's covered in chapter eight. And if you have the proper attitude toward market movements, it's an enormous help in securities.

    And the final chapter is on the margin of safety, which means, don't try and drive a 9,800-pound truck over a bridge that claims it's, you know, "Capacity: 10,000 pounds." But go down the road a little bit and find one that says, "Capacity: 15,000 pounds.".

    #50511. Gold's bad year is getting worse. Why its price keeps falling

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1471 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 CNBC ↗ Open Full Page

    Gold's bad year is getting worse. Why its price keeps falling

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1471 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Precious metals investors can be forgiven if they feel like the past year has given them whiplash.
    • According to recent reports, following a torrid run, which saw the price of gold hit new records 53 times in 2025, gold hit a historic high of $5,589.38 an ounce on Jan.
    • It has been revealed that A convergence of factors pushed gold to historic highs earlier this year, according to Suki Cooper, global head of commodities research at Standard Chartered, the London-based multinational bank.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Precious metals investors can be forgiven if they feel like the past year has given them whiplash.

    According to recent reports, following a torrid run, which saw the price of gold hit new records 53 times in 2025, gold hit a historic high of $5,589.38 an ounce on Jan. 28, only to take an almost equally historic nosedive. On Wednesday, gold fell below $3,800 for the first time since September 2025, roughly a third below its peak.

    It has been revealed that A convergence of factors pushed gold to historic highs earlier this year, according to Suki Cooper, global head of commodities research at Standard Chartered, the London-based multinational bank. Now a different convergence is bringing the price down.

    "Gold can behave as a commodity or a currency," Cooper mentioned.

    Which role it plays depends on the factors dominating the market and the psyche of investors, and right now, it's the currency argument that is bringing the precious metal down.

    Cooper said gold's climb began with strong physical demand that started in 2022 and raised the floor under prices. A second phase followed as investors rethought gold's place in their portfolios. With the cost of holding a non-yielding asset falling, they started thinking about the metal for the longer term. That, Cooper said, marked a turnaround.

    Until early 2025, Cooper mentioned, long-term investors, especially those in gold-backed exchange-traded funds, had been cutting their exposure, which effectively added supply to the market. Last year, that reversed: ETF holdings, led by the SPDR Gold Shares (GLD), rose by roughly 800 tons and helped absorb the market's excess supply.

    "There was a lot of one-way interest, a lot of appetite to buy but not to sell," Cooper said.

    Recent findings suggest that with selling in the secondary market staying muted, prices kept rising. By the end of 2025, net ETF holdings had passed 4,000 tons. Globally, gold ETFs had their strongest year ever for inflows, $89 billion, led by North America, according to the World Gold Council, with assets more than doubling to $559 billion in total.

    A weaker dollar, lower bond yields and worries about global debt "set the foundation for gold to hit highs in 2026," Cooper remarked.

    Investors who had been under-exposed to the metal kept buying.

    Evan Mills, a financial advisor with Scholar Financial Advising, a fee-only firm in Winston-Salem, N.C., mentioned the lower interest rates, expectations of further rate cuts and a weakening dollar, were all reasons for investors to favor gold.

    Industry observers note that "It was a perfect spot to be in if you were an investor in gold and commodities as a whole," Mills mentioned. And investors did extremely well, especially with lower interest rates. "Cash doesn't do well in that environment, so a lot of people looked toward other places to hold their cash and maintain purchasing power," Mills said.

    Sources indicate that the speed of the rally made some investors uneasy, and there was growing talk that the Fed could tighten. Then, Cooper noted, the Middle East conflict broke out and gold changed roles. It stopped acting as a portfolio safe haven and became "a liquidity provider.".

    Cooper explained that because it was liquid and easy to sell, investors sold it to raise cash, which set off the first correction. Since then, she stated, markets have been pricing in what the Fed will do.

    "In 2026, the Fed has leaned more toward higher interest rates," Mills said.

    This week, the Federal Reserve Board of Governors member Christopher Waller said a 50-basis point rate hike may be necessary to "shock people.".

    "There are higher Treasury yields and a strengthening dollar, so the opportunity cost of holding an asset that doesn't produce income is much higher," Mills said.

    Mills said that in the current situation, gold investors are missing out on an environment in which cash actually does well, with money market funds that can pay 4% to 5%.

    "Cash maintains purchasing power, and you don't need to put it in an illiquid asset or one where you're relying on another person to see the value," Mills noted.

    From 2025 to 2026, gold didn't become any less scarce; the alternatives to owning it became more attractive.

    "Stocks, bonds, the classic portfolio mix, all became a lot more attractive, so people looked at the opportunity cost and decided it wasn't worth holding gold anymore," Mills mentioned.

    This has been the case for other metals in 2026 as well, with silver plummeting from an all-time high price.

    Sources indicate that after an extraordinary rally, it's easy to start questioning gold. Mills said investors should start by remembering that expectations were extremely high. "When expectations are 20% or 30% returns in a year, then of course when returns drop, people start to panic," Mills said.

    Panic shouldn't be the watchword for gold investors, but caution should remain.

    "In the short term, with real yields going up and the dollar likely strengthening with future Fed hikes, I'd be cautious about gold in the overall portfolio," Mills remarked.

    For investors, the key is to understand why gold is in your portfolio to begin with.

    "If you're looking for it to be a short-term purchase, then gold likely doesn't belong in your portfolio at all," Mills noted. If the metal is seen as a hedge, gold can remain a valuable part of a portfolio, but it can still be a poor investment depending on the price you pay to get in.

    "If you're looking at gold to be the growth section of your portfolio, you're likely going to be disappointed," he noted. "Gold is insurance, not an engine, and the mistake is buying insurance when its price has skyrocketed," he added.

    For investors who bought at January's peak as a modest, long-term hedge, a sharp downturn doesn't defeat the purpose, he mentioned. "You have nothing to really worry about, because that's what the whole goal of gold was.".

    Gold tends to do well when the dollar weakens or when markets and geopolitics turn uncertain, Mills said, and when those pressures fade, the rest of a portfolio should pick up the slack.

    It has been revealed that "That's the whole point of insurance, and the whole point of diversification," he stated. "Gold does well when the other parts of your portfolio might be slacking, and when they flip-flop, that's a good thing.".

    Other commodities experts say gold remains a good long-term bet. Amy Gower, head of metals and mining strategy at Morgan Stanley, told CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe" that there are "still lots of reasons" for investors to hang on to their gold despite the correction this year.

    According to recent reports, philip Diehl, former director of the U.S. Mint and now president of U.S. Money Reserve, an Austin, Texas-based distributor of government-issued gold, silver and platinum coins, stated the long-term case for gold is still in place, but the combination of abrupt shifts in U.S. trade policy and geopolitical alliances, along with the Iran war, qualifies as a black swan event for the precious metal.

    In a recent development, "The fundamentals that drove that bull market remain in place. They were interrupted by the Cat 5 hurricane that was unleashed in the Persian Gulf in an unwise war," Diehl stated.

    He expects that to change after American voters "issued a mandate" to end that war two weeks ago.

    "I'm confident gold prices will return to their upward trajectory in 2027 as oil prices normalize and prices fall at the pump, allowing interest rates to stabilize," Diehl mentioned.

    Central banks continue to buy gold, with the highest monthly total in September, according to the World Gold Council, though overall purchasing is 7% lower than the same period last year.

    Sources indicate that marc Chandler, managing partner and chief market strategist at Bannockburn Capital Markets, stated surveys suggest that, in aggregate, that will not change. "However, don't only think about China or U.S. rivals," Chandler said, noting that the World Gold Council has identified Poland, a NATO member, as one of the larger buyers for most of this year.

    "Retail has been burned," Chandler remarked. "Higher interest rates have made non-interest-bearing assets less attractive, including bitcoin.".

    In a recent development, chandler said that the price of gold is headed to $3,500 to $3,600. Gold hit a fresh low below $3,700 on Thursday morning.

    Sources indicate that "There is nothing on the charts that states a low is in place," Chandler said. "For the anxious bottom pickers, I urge caution and being patient to see some reversal pattern. For the most part, the decline looks fairly orderly.".

    "Gold is still very expensive compared to anything but the last two years," Chandler mentioned, noting that gold's 10-year (120-month) moving average is about $2,127 and its 20-year (240-month) moving average is about $1,666.

    #50506. Breaking: What Ron Johnson's 'Ponzi scheme' label gets wrong about Social Security, experts say

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1273 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 CNBC ↗ Open Full Page

    Breaking: What Ron Johnson's 'Ponzi scheme' label gets wrong about Social Security, experts say

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1273 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • A newly introduced Senate budget committee hearing on Wednesday reignited an old Social Security question: Is the program, which provides monthly benefits to millions of Americans, a Ponzi scheme?
    • Senate Budget Committee Chairman Ron Johnson, a Republican representing Wisconsin, called Social Security "a legal Ponzi scheme" in his opening remarks.
    • Sources indicate that A Ponzi scheme is an investment fraud that uses funds from newly introduced investors to pay existing investors, according to the Securities and Exchange Commission, Johnson wrote in his chairman's hearing memo.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    A newly introduced Senate budget committee hearing on Wednesday reignited an old Social Security question: Is the program, which provides monthly benefits to millions of Americans, a Ponzi scheme?

    Senate Budget Committee Chairman Ron Johnson, a Republican representing Wisconsin, called Social Security "a legal Ponzi scheme" in his opening remarks. But experts say his comments overlook how Social Security works and the real dilemma for lawmakers over its looming funding shortfall.

    Sources indicate that A Ponzi scheme is an investment fraud that uses funds from newly introduced investors to pay existing investors, according to the Securities and Exchange Commission, Johnson wrote in his chairman's hearing memo. He mentioned that Social Security fits the description if you remove the word "fraud.".

    Johnson's comments followed his Wednesday morning interview on Fox Business, where he said, "At this point, there's really no way to fix Social Security.".

    "You can't fix it, you just shut it down and then hope that you can recover some of your money," Johnson said during the Fox Business interview.

    "As far as I can tell, this is the first time in decades that a senior senator, chairman of the budget committee, stated he would rather shut down Social Security than fix it," Sen. Ron Wyden, D-Ore., said during the hearing.

    At the Senate hearing, Johnson mentioned his comments during the TV interview were "imprecise" and that he was talking broadly about Ponzi schemes, not Social Security, that need to be shut down.

    Johnson mentioned he wants lawmakers to pass a law to ensure seniors' Social Security benefits are not reduced, "then roll up our sleeves and fix the real problem, which is $24 trillion of 10-year deficits.".

    The Congressional Budget Office has projected a $24.4 trillion cumulative federal budget deficit over the next 10 years.

    Johnson proposed a bill on Wednesday that would allow for Social Security retirement benefits to be funded by general revenue once that trust fund reaches its insolvency date.

    Critics say that's not a viable solution. Using the general fund to pay for Social Security would "absolutely explode the national debt" and cost 165% of gross domestic product over 75 years, Maya MacGuineas, president of the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget, a nonpartisan organization, noted in a statement.

    The way Johnson described the program during the hearing was "out of touch with the way the American public understands and knows Social Security," stated Bill Sweeney, senior vice president of government affairs at AARP, a nonprofit, nonpartisan organization representing Americans age 50 and over.

    Recent findings suggest that "The budget committee should know that Social Security is not part of the budget," Sweeney stated. "It runs on its own budget.".

    According to recent reports, social Security does affect the unified federal deficit and debt held by the public when outlays exceed dedicated revenues, according to CBO. The Treasury securities held by Social Security's trust funds count as intragovernmental debt, which is included in gross federal debt but not in debt held by the public.

    Social Security benefits are mainly funded by payroll tax contributions. When the program's income exceeds its costs, the surplus is invested in special U.S. Treasury securities held in the trust funds.

    Social Security is not allowed to borrow money and cannot go into debt, according to Sweeney.

    "It's never contributed a penny to the debt," Sweeney said. "It's not part of the national debt because it's in a separate budget.".

    In a recent development, social Security's trust funds may be depleted within the next six to eight years, based on current projections. If that happens, Social Security benefits may be cut.

    In a recent development, in six years — the fourth quarter of 2032 — the Social Security retirement trust fund may run out, Social Security's trustees projected in June. At that time, 78% of those benefits would be payable.

    In eight years — the third quarter of 2034 — Social Security's combined retirement and disability trust funds may run out, when 83% of scheduled benefits would be payable, according to the Social Security trustees' projections.

    Had payroll tax revenue kept up with gross domestic product over the past four decades, the program would be able to pay full benefits until 2059 — an additional 25 years versus current projections, according to recent AARP research.

    At the hearing, Johnson held up a picture of the trust funds, which he said is a "four-drawer file in Parkersburg, West Virginia.".

    Johnson similarly mentioned the trust fund files at a July 2023 hearing. In 2005, then-President George W. Bush was shown paper evidence of Social Security's U.S. bonds during a visit to the Bureau of Public Debt in Parkersburg.

    While the politicians' actions seem to suggest the trust funds aren't real, experts say they are legitimate.

    In a recent development, "It's all about trying to scare people into thinking that Social Security is not going to be there for you when it's time for you to retire," Sweeney noted. "For 91 years it has been, and there's no reason to believe it won't be.".

    Wednesday's Senate hearing was a "missed opportunity" for a more in-depth discussion of the challenges facing Social Security, remarked Jason Fichtner, a witness at the hearing and executive director of the LIMRA Retirement Income Institute, a research initiative within the insurance trade association LIMRA.

    Plans such as raising or eliminating the taxable maximum for payroll contributions to Social Security may push the program's funding woes 20 or 30 years later, but would not make the program solvent for the 75-year target, according to Fichtner, a former Social Security Administration official.

    Moreover, fixing Social Security would not resolve the government's larger fiscal complications, which would still leave the economy vulnerable to bond market strain, he mentioned.

    It has been revealed that "The other concern is fear," Fichtner said. "We do see evidence now of people claiming Social Security earlier because of their fear of the trust funds running out of money or Social Security not being able to pay benefits.".

    A June 2025 AARP survey found 49% of respondents who had recently claimed or planned to claim Social Security benefits earlier than planned were mostly motivated by concerns the program may run out of money.

    "Social Security is very effective at solving problems, and it's a thorn in the side of the federal government because they have done a horrible job managing so many aspects of our finances," said labor economist Kathryn Anne Edwards, a witness at the hearing and a senior fellow at the National Academy of Social Insurance, a provider of research and policy analysis on social insurance and economic security programs.

    "But Americans don't see it that way," she remarked.

    More than half of Social Security recipients surveyed say benefits are their main source of income, according to an August AARP poll.

    Social Security reform provides an opportunity to expand the program to help meet Americans' needs, Edwards remarked. Adding universal paid family and medical leave to the program could help individuals and families who don't currently have access to those benefits, she said. Moreover, strengthening unemployment insurance could help ensure financial security amid the prospect of AI-related job losses, Edwards said.

    In a recent development, senators who were elected on Nov. 3 will be in office when the retirement trust fund depletion date hits in 2032. The next session of Congress may provide an opportunity for "serious" hearings on the future of Social Security, Sweeney noted.

    The Senate budget committee's Wednesday hearing followed other recent hearings on the program's future, including a June Senate finance subcommittee hearing and an August Senate finance full committee hearing.

    #50502. Industry News: Netflix, Amazon, Fox to bid for 2030 men's World Cup rights; Disney out

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (539 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 CNBC ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: Netflix, Amazon, Fox to bid for 2030 men's World Cup rights; Disney out

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (539 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that netflix, Amazon, YouTube and Fox are all expected to submit offers to win the U.S.
    • Fox and NBCU's Telemundo are the incumbent rights holders.
    • CNBC previously reported that media executives are planning on the winning bid coming in around $1.5 billion — or maybe even higher — although that amount could vary somewhat depending on whether both 2030 and 2034 are acquired.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that netflix, Amazon, YouTube and Fox are all expected to submit offers to win the U.S. media rights for the 2030 men's World Cup before today's deadline, according to people familiar with the matter — but Disney will not be putting in a bid.

    Fox and NBCU's Telemundo are the incumbent rights holders. FIFA would prefer to sell both the English and Spanish rights together, to one buyer, for the 2030 World Cup, to be held in Spain, Portugal and Morocco. Media companies also have the right to bid on the 2034 World Cup, which will be held in Saudi Arabia.

    CNBC previously reported that media executives are planning on the winning bid coming in around $1.5 billion — or maybe even higher — although that amount could vary somewhat depending on whether both 2030 and 2034 are acquired.

    Sources indicate that FIFA is open to the idea of a potential partnership bid in which rights are split between a traditional broadcaster and a streamer, to maximize reach. Still, unlike in other countries where there are government mandates on airing games for free, FIFA will not mandate that a subscription streamer sublicense games. That decision will be up to the winning bidder.

    In a recent development, FIFA is satisfied that enough people in the U.S. already have a Netflix or Amazon Prime Video subscription that reach won't be an issue, according to people familiar with the matter. The 2027 Women's World Cup will be on Netflix in the U.S., and Netflix looks to air all of the games without a partner.

    Sources indicate that disney/ESPN will not be bidding, according to people familiar with the matter. ESPN Chairman Jimmy Pitaro said he was interested in World Cup rights earlier this year at CNBC Sport x Boardroom's Game Proposal Summit.

    Recent findings suggest that in recent weeks, ESPN ran the numbers and couldn't get to $1.5 billion or higher while also having to save money for NHL, MLB and European soccer — English Premier League and Champions League — all of which will likely renew their media rights deals in 2027, remarked the people, who asked not to be named because the discussions were private. ESPN looked into entering a bid with a partner but ultimately decided not to bid, one of the people said.

    NBCUniversal still hasn't made a decision on bidding, potentially putting Telemundo in jeopardy of losing the games for 2030, according to a person familiar with the matter. NBCUniversal has already spent billions on NBA and also needs to save money for both MLB and EPL potentially as well as the NFL, which will likely be a 2028 negotiation.

    Skydance and Apple will not bid, according to people familiar with the matter.

    A FIFA spokesperson declined to comment, citing confidentiality of the tender process.

    FIFA executives plan to travel to the U.S. next week to meet personally with bidders to assess their bids and potentially get final offers. FIFA intends to choose a winner before the end of the year.

    The CNBC Sport newsletter with Alex Sherman brings you the biggest news and exclusive interviews from the worlds of sports business and media, delivered weekly to your inbox.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Two weeks ago, Monique Griffin got a troubling email.

    The French drugmaker Sanofi told her that a shipping delay had interrupted supply of the drug that she relies on to manage her rare muscle-wasting disease. Her next infusion was canceled. Griffin, who is 51 and uses a wheelchair due to Pompe disease, fears what will happen if the shortage isn't resolved soon.

    "You're basically letting the disease take over again," she noted. "It's terrifying.".

    According to recent reports, more than three months after initial reports of supply problems with treatments for Pompe disease, the disruption drags on, with more patients learning their infusions have been canceled. Sanofi remarked it has made progress restoring the supply to patients in some countries, but added that shipping delays could interrupt infusions for some U.S. patients through the end of November.

    A Sanofi spokesperson noted there were no problems with drug quality and the manufacturer is "committed to ensuring that the most vulnerable patients receive treatment first during this period." The company added that patients should speak with a health professional before taking another treatment, adding, "these medicines are not interchangeable.".

    In a statement, the Food and Drug Administration said "patient access to these treatments is a priority for the agency and we have offered our assistance to Sanofi on anything needed to help ensure all patient needs are met.".

    About one in every 19,000 babies is born with Pompe disease, which is named after the Dutch pathologist who discovered the condition nearly a century ago.

    Industry observers note that patients lack an enzyme for breaking down a complex sugar, causing a toxic buildup of glycogen inside their cells. Their muscles weaken and their heart can become enlarged. They have trouble breathing and eating. Left untreated, the disease is often fatal.

    Sources indicate that sanofi's Lumizyme and a second-generation version, Nexviazyme, replace the missing enzyme, protecting the patient's muscles. Patients typically receive Sanofi's drugs every two weeks.

    "It's a lifeline," stated Jenna Yarborough, a rare disease advocate whose two children with Pompe disease have not been affected by the drug shortage.

    While Pompe disease patients rely on Sanofi's drugs, several other treatments have entered clinical trials, including separate gene therapies from AskBio and Astellas Pharma.

    Sanofi notes the drug shortage is the result of issues at its manufacturing facility in Ireland, which public documents show the tech giant has known about for several months. The FDA inspected the plant between January 12 and January 20, 2026 and found violations involving two unrelated drugs. The company began responding to the violations in February, but on June 22, the FDA sent the company a warning letter saying it had still not addressed the "underlying failure" to comply with manufacturing requirements. Addressing the FDA's ongoing concerns has contributed to the supply disruption of the Pompe therapies, according to Sanofi.

    There's a sense of frustration within the Pompe community that the company did not do enough to warn patients about the potential for a supply disruption. Ryan Colburn, a person living with Pompe who is active in the advocacy space, states many patients were unaware of the manufacturing problems at Sanofi and were left with no way to prepare for them. "The lack of proactive transparency and apparent lack of buffer are of huge concern for any medicine that people's lives and well-being depend on access to," Colburn said.

    A spokesperson for Sanofi responded, "As the situation evolved, and the extent of the disruption became clearer, we engaged global and U.S. patient advocacy organizations, patients and clinicians to inform them, and we have worked to continue to keep these groups and individuals updated through regular communications. We remain committed to continuity of care and to transparent, ongoing communication with the Pompe community as we work to stabilize supply.".

    Chelsey McGee's 10-year-old son Logan has taken Lumizyme every two weeks since he was diagnosed with Pompe disease as an infant. While his infusions haven't been canceled yet, she's concerned that missing even one appointment will damage his heart. Sanofi's drug has kept him healthy enough to play soccer.

    "It's important that we stay on his timeline and keep his heart healthy," she said.

    Industry observers note that mcGee, who lives in Minneapolis, is frustrated by what she says is a lack of transparency from Sanofi. She discovered the FDA cited the pharmaceutical company for manufacturing problems by searching the agency's website, not from the company.

    It has been revealed that griffin, who lives in Orlando, has taken Lumizyme since 2010 when she was diagnosed with an adult-onset version of the disease. The diagnosis came after she became so fatigued that she fell while carrying groceries and suffered a concussion.

    She knows what it's like to go without her infusions. She missed a few appointments earlier this year due to an insurance mix-up. She likened it to having "a really bad flu." She became extremely fatigued, struggled to breathe and started to feel pain in her legs, arms and back.

    Pompe is a progressive disease, meaning it gets worse over time. She worries most about losing the strength to breathe. She sleeps with assisted ventilation.

    She works in the theme parks industry and is hoping to attend a conference this week. While her Lumizyme infusions remain on hold, she hopes to get through the week of meetings "on caffeine and goodwill.".

    3-step method to influence people and win them over, from a Stanford expert: ‘Your voice is like a muscle’

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Think back on the most memorable, inspiring speeches or presentations you've witnessed.
    • "The human brain is designed to pick out and focus on things that are novel and new," says Abrahams, a Stanford University lecturer on strategic communication and host of the "Think Fast, Talk Smart" podcast.
    • Indeed, successful leaders often have an uncanny ability to win over a crowd: The power of persuasion lies not just in what you actually have to say, but also in how you say it, research demonstrates.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Think back on the most memorable, inspiring speeches or presentations you've witnessed. They probably weren't delivered in a monotone, Matt Abrahams says.

    "The human brain is designed to pick out and focus on things that are novel and new," says Abrahams, a Stanford University lecturer on strategic communication and host of the "Think Fast, Talk Smart" podcast. "So anything that stays the same, like a monotonous voice or cadence, we don't pay as much attention to.".

    Indeed, successful leaders often have an uncanny ability to win over a crowd: The power of persuasion lies not just in what you actually have to say, but also in how you say it, research demonstrates. The topic has taken on new relevance this week as Nvidia interim CEO Colette Kress steps into one of the most closely watched leadership roles in corporate America.

    In appearances this week, including Nvidia's quarterly earnings call and an interview with CNBC's "Mad Money" host Jim Cramer, Kress has discussed the tech giant's performance. She's also addressed employees and investors in a time of leadership upheaval, following Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang's high-profile resignation on Nov. 12.

    In a recent development, how Kress communicates has drawn attention and, in some circles, criticism. On Wednesday, The Wall Street Journal described her public speaking style as "slow, steady, almost monotone." That doesn't necessarily make it ineffective. Her situation, however, highlights a broader challenge leaders face when they need to inform, reassure and persuade large groups of people at once.

    Recent findings suggest that generally speaking, anyone can stand a better chance at persuading others to follow them by honing an engaging speaking style, says Abrahams. Some people may be naturally expressive and engaging. For others, it's a skill that requires time and practice.

    Abrahams suggests a three-step playbook for anyone learning to speak more persuasively: "repetition, reflection and feedback.".

    Abrahams' simplest advice for making yourself a more engaging speaker: "When you're using emotive words, reflect the emotion in them." That means adding some emphasis to words like "exciting," "huge" or "challenging," and so on. If you tend to speak monotonously, leaning into obviously emotive words can help you vary your tone and inflection enough to keep your audience's attention.

    In a recent development, there's a catch, of course: People find inauthenticity off-putting and disingenuous, notes Abrahams. Don't alter your voice entirely, he suggests — just add some variety to your intonation and speaking volume. Learning to do so while still sounding natural takes practice, he notes.

    According to recent reports, "Your voice is like a muscle," says Abrahams. "You can train it. You can grow it [and] strengthen it, just like you go to the gym to lift weights.".

    Industry observers note that practicing repetition starts with reading aloud from a chosen text, which Abrahams recommends so you don't have to overthink what you're saying. And the same way you might lift heavy weights to get stronger, Abrahams suggests reading overly expressive material to start getting out of your comfort zone and practice being energetic and engaging. He instructs his Stanford students to try reading Dr. Seuss books, as their playful words and bouncy rhymes can naturally make for a lively performance.

    Industry observers note that while practicing reading out loud, record yourself to watch and listen to later, Abrahams recommends. Then, use the recording to reflect on what works and what doesn't, and incorporate your self-feedback into your next reading. You can also play the recording for a few trusted peers to get their thoughts, Abrahams notes.

    It has been revealed that if a line reading doesn't sound natural in your voice, feels flat or even rushed, keep trying it until you're satisfied, he notes. Leaders are often asked to deliver lengthy speeches or talk for long periods in interviews and panels, so it's key to build your vocal stamina, he adds.

    "We have to calibrate ourselves," he says.

    Abrahams asks his Stanford graduate students to review their recordings in three ways, he says:.

    "That's how you train your brain to see: 'What do I need to sound like?'" notes Abrahams.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Payward, the owner of crypto exchange Kraken, is pushing into private markets with its latest acquisition, underscoring a broader shift in cryptocurrencies, from trading-led growth to the buildout of financial infrastructure.
    • Sources indicate that payward said late Wednesday that it's buying venture capital and asset management provider Tribe Capital Management, led by Payward's co-CEO Arjun Sethi.
    • Tribe, where Sethi is co-founder and chairman, invests across early- and late-stage private companies and has $2.7 billion in assets under management.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Payward, the owner of crypto exchange Kraken, is pushing into private markets with its latest acquisition, underscoring a broader shift in cryptocurrencies, from trading-led growth to the buildout of financial infrastructure.

    Sources indicate that payward said late Wednesday that it's buying venture capital and asset management provider Tribe Capital Management, led by Payward's co-CEO Arjun Sethi. No purchase price was disclosed.

    Tribe, where Sethi is co-founder and chairman, invests across early- and late-stage private companies and has $2.7 billion in assets under management.

    In a recent development, "Joining Payward gives us the opportunity to bring Tribe's investment approach to a global financial platform," Jonathan Hsu, another co-founder of Tribe Capital, stated in a statement. "We see a strong fit between our investment approach and Payward's infrastructure, distribution, and product-building capabilities.".

    Payward didn't respond to a request for comment.

    The acquisition is novel among crypto exchanges. Unlike exchange-owned venture arms such as Coinbase Ventures or Binance Labs, Payward is looking to integrate Tribe's investment and fund-management capabilities into an existing custody, trading, collateral and tokenization infrastructure to develop private-market investment products.

    Payward is trying to position itself to capture value from a broader crypto-driven transformation of financial services, not use the venture vehicle to draw more capital into the crypto ecosystem.

    According to recent reports, the acquisition is another step in the evolution in the crypto exchange business model. With cryptocurrency prices continuing to decline this year, crypto exchanges have worked to move past their reliance on trading volumes and transaction fees, focusing instead on building the infrastructure connecting digital assets with traditional finance.

    #50475. Amid recent banking outages, should you start carrying cash again? Top advisors weigh in

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (846 w)
    📖 Baca
    General 📈 Bullish 🌐 CNBC ↗ Open Full Page

    Amid recent banking outages, should you start carrying cash again? Top advisors weigh in

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (846 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • For years, Americans have moved away from using physical U.S.
    • Sources indicate that JPMorgan Chase on Monday reported a technical matter that disrupted some consumer banking services, with ripple effects extending to several major U.S.
    • Those reports came on the heels of separate, widespread concerns with Microsoft Outlook and communication systems used by air traffic control centers.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    For years, Americans have moved away from using physical U.S. currency in favor of credit, debit and digital payments. But amid the recent outages affecting some consumer banking services, experts say it's wise to revisit cash.

    Sources indicate that JPMorgan Chase on Monday reported a technical matter that disrupted some consumer banking services, with ripple effects extending to several major U.S. banks and the peer-to-peer payments network Zelle. A day later, a separate outage affected Apple, temporarily disrupting Apple Pay and iCloud, the service that keeps data available across various Apple devices.

    Those reports came on the heels of separate, widespread concerns with Microsoft Outlook and communication systems used by air traffic control centers.

    In a recent development, as technology outages expose vulnerabilities across parts of the U.S. economy, some top advisors say consumers should reconsider keeping physical money on hand.

    "This is about preparedness, not panic," noted David La Placa, CEO of Intellectus Partners in San Francisco, which ranked No. 92 on CNBC's Financial Advisor 100 list for 2026. "I think keeping some cash at home is a reasonable starting point for many households.".

    La Placa advises consumers to "build redundancy" into their financial lives.

    "Maintain access to at least a second financial institution, keep a backup credit card from a different issuer and make sure you have more than one way to access liquidity," he said.

    In a recent development, A client's cash management should be diversified, mentioned Seth Fierston, a certified financial planner and co-president of Fierston Financial Group in West Hartford, Connecticut. The firm ranked No. 22 on CNBC's Financial Advisor 100 list.

    Industry observers note that having multiple accounts at brokerages or banks and various ways to move money, including Automated Clearing House, or ACH, wire, check, Venmo or Zelle, "can help mitigate technology risk," Fierston said. "One of our guiding principles is flexibility.".

    When it comes to everyday transactions, Americans are increasingly relying on digital forms of payment.

    These days, only about 46% of Americans carry cash with them always or most of the time, according to a survey of nearly 10,000 adults conducted between May and June by the Pew Research Center, a nonpartisan research group.

    Roughly 42% of U.S. adults said they don't use cash for any purchases in a typical week, up from 24% in 2015, Pew found.

    Sources indicate that young adults are the least likely to carry physical currency. Among adults under 30, 51% stated they go completely cashless, according to the survey.

    "I recommend to my clients that they always keep three days of average cash spend on hand given the uncertainty of life in general," mentioned Tim Lootens, CFP, managing director at Chilton Capital Management in Houston, which ranked No. 7 on this year's Financial Advisor 100.

    Considering the recent technical troubles, Lootens remarked consumers should keep even more cash at the ready.

    Sources indicate that "We've had the Microsoft Outlook outage, the FAA ground shutdown and now banking disruption," he said. "This makes me think five to seven days may be a better number.".

    According to recent reports, the right amount is as psychological as it is financial, he added. "The ability to access cash and having comfort knowing it is there when needed is so key," he said.

    Brian Vendig, president and chief investment officer at MJP Wealth Advisors, which ranked No. 42 on CNBC's Financial Advisor 100, also said he recommends holding a dollar amount that corresponds with a household's discretionary living expenses. He advised having enough for at least one to two weeks, depending on their needs.

    While there is little precedent for a banking or payment system outage lasting more than a few business days, Vendig said, a one- to two-week cash reserve provides a "reasonable buffer" for essentials such as groceries, gas and other necessities, if electronic payments become unavailable.

    "We apply this range because it is also an emotional concern for most people, and they might want to have a little extra saved at home due to the size of their household and having a little extra 'peace of mind' guarantee," he said.

    Vendig mentioned he recommends stashing extra cash in a secure location at home for emergency needs.

    Vendig also said consumers should be vigilant in ensuring their electronic devices have the most recent software security patches installed.

    Criminals will try to exploit moments of uncertainty, experts say.

    "Consumers should assume they will be targeted," said Craig Timm, senior director of anti-money laundering at ACAMS, an anti-financial crime group.

    It has been revealed that "[This week's] reported bank outages are likely to cause widespread confusion and fear among consumers about losing access to their money," he said. "Criminals will try to exploit that anxiety by pushing victims to take urgent action to protect their funds or restore account access.".

    Recent findings suggest that as always, "stay alert, never click on links in unexpected bank messages and never share personal information such as passwords or PINs," he advised. "If you need to reach your bank, use a trusted, official channel," Timm mentioned.
